Strictly speaking, no one vampire has "the three pricus (sic) votes", since
it's a bloc vote. But if there are no Prisci on the table except for ex-
Priscus Gratiano, his special ability (which remains absent his Priscus
title) gives him a vote (the only vote) in the Prisci sub-referendum, and
therefore control over the disposition of the 3 votes of the Priscus
bloc. They're not 'his' votes, since he's not casting them directly, but
he does have effective control over their disposition in the absence of
any Prisci.

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <93l7e4$qff$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>, <X_Ze...@email.msn.com> wrote:

>You are so Priscocious. BTW, Isn't it also true that while Gratiano
>retains his one vote in the Pricus subvote. It still requires a Pricus
>to call the Pricus vote. In other words, If Gratiano becomes a Cardinal
>and there are no other Pricus in play then Gratiano's special has no
>effect.

Not true. 6.3.3 reads in part:

"The Prisci Block: The prisci [...] as a group have three votes. During a
referendum, the prisci block of three votes is cast 'for' or 'against' the
referendum according to the prisci sub-referendum. Each ready priscus provides
one vote for this sub-referendum, and no other votes may be used in this
sub-referendum. Each vote is either 'for' or 'against' the main referendum.
Whichever side has the greater number of votes in the sub-referendum gains
three votes in the main referendum. If the sub-referendum is tied, the
prisci abstain from the main vote. As prisci cast their votes in the sub-
referendum, the prisci block of three votes may shift between 'for,'
'against' (sic*) and 'abstain' (as the majority in the sub-referendum
changes)."

Nothing about requiring a Priscus to have a Prisci vote. Ordinarily, only
Prisci get to vote in it, but Gratiano's special overrides that. If there
are no Prisci, you still have a Priscus subvote in every referendum, but it's
a null section.

<fre...@netcom.com> writes

>I don't know what they're teaching in the U.K. but in the U.S. they state that
>such a comma is optional. I usually see it more often than not and always

Whilst people use commas all over the place, there seems to be a
stylistic tendency to not use a comma before the "and". This alters,
somewhat, when you start enumerating lists with semi-colons (most often
found when one of the elements contains a comma, or where the use of the
comma might be somewhat confusing).

It seems to be most common for publishers to *not* use the comma before
the "and", and publishers tend to define one house-style and stick to
it, so that when you pick up a copy of The New York Times, you know you
are reading The New York Times and not, for example, the Daily Planet
based solely on its style, regardless of content.

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <20010113051053...@ng-fl1.aol.com>,
Halcyan 2 <halc...@aol.com> wrote:

>And don't the British have billion and trillion reversed (compared to the
>U.S.)?

Not reversed as such, but the British system is more comfortable, as it's
consistent. The US uses 'billion' when it means 'thousand million':

one (10^0)
ten (ten ones) (10^1)
hundred (ten tens) (10^2)
thousand (ten hundreds) (10^3)
million (a thousand thousands) (10^6)
US-billion (a thousand millions) (10^9)
UK-billion, US-trillion (a million millions) (10^12)
US-quadrillion (a thousand UK-billions) (10^15)
US-quintillion (a million UK-billions) (10^18)
US-sextillion (a thousand million UK-billions) (10^21)
UK-trillion, US-septillion (a UK-billion UK-billions) (10^24)

The difference between the systems is that the US adds an ordinal
('tri' to 'quad,' for example) every 3 powers of 10 (as in 10^6 to
10^9), and the UK system only adds an ordinal when the power of 10 is
twice that of the old ordinal (10^6 to 10^12, then to 10^24). Since you
already have perfectly good names for the smaller numbers, the UK
system is to my mind more elegant, if only because you only have to go
up to UK-trillion for any discussion of magnitudes outside the more rarefied
realms of science, whereas you have to get into goofy-sounding names
like "septillion" to accomplish the same with the US system.

In article <3A5FAB3F...@netcom.com>,
Frederick Scott <fre...@netcom.com> wrote:

>I don't know what they're teaching in the U.K. but in the U.S. they state that
>such a comma is optional. I usually see it more often than not and always
>use it, myself.

For instance, in the following sentence:

"This book is dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand and God."

It's pretty clear that a comma after "Ayn Rand" would drastically change
the meaning of the sentence. One sentence is ambiguous and can be interpreted
to mean that the writer's parents are Ayn Rand and God. With the comma
in place, the sense of the sentence as enumerating three distinct entities
to thank (parents/Ayn Rand/God) rather than a single set (parents=Ayn Rand &
God).

The serial comma: just a good idea, not the law. But a good idea
nonetheless.

gomi
